h1: Criminal Record Expungement Lawyer El Paso, TX
intro: An arrest or an old deferred case can follow you into every background check in El Paso — Fort Bliss, the ports of entry, the hospitals, the school districts. Texas gives you two ways to clear it, and attorney Robert Navar helps you find out which one you qualify for.
summaryHeading: Two ways to clear a Texas record — and how the case ended decides which
summary: An expunction under the Code of Criminal Procedure's expunction chapter destroys the record — the arrest, the charge and the court file — and in general lets you lawfully deny it happened.
An order of nondisclosure under Government Code Chapter 411, Subchapter E-1 seals the record from the public and private employers, while police and licensing agencies can still see it.

Generally, expunction fits dismissed cases, acquittals and completed Class C deferred dispositions; nondisclosure fits completed deferred adjudication and some convictions. Eligibility turns on the offense, the outcome and waiting periods.
The consultation is free and the work is flat-fee after we confirm eligibility. Schedule a records review or call 915-503-1600.

sections.heading: Destroy It or Seal It: What Each Remedy Actually Does
paragraphs: People use "expunge" for everything, but Texas has two distinct tools and they do different things. An expunction is an order under the Code of Criminal Procedure's expunction chapter — Chapter 55, recodified as Chapter 55A in 2025 — directing every agency that holds the record (the arresting department, the clerk, the prosecutor, DPS) to delete or return it. Once the order is final, you may in general deny the arrest on most applications. It is the stronger remedy, and it is limited to cases that ended without a conviction: a dismissal, an acquittal, a no-bill, or a completed Class C deferred disposition.

An order of nondisclosure under Government Code Chapter 411, Subchapter E-1 does not destroy anything. It prohibits the clerk and DPS from releasing the record to the public, so a private employer, landlord or background-check company does not see it. Law enforcement, prosecutors, and certain licensing agencies — nursing, teaching, law enforcement certification — still can. Nondisclosure is the remedy for many completed deferred adjudications and for certain first misdemeanor convictions, generally after a waiting period that depends on the offense. Which one you need is dictated by how the case ended, not by preference — and some El Paso clients discover the deferred case they thought was merely "dismissed" is eligible for the stronger remedy.

sections.heading: Sorting Your History Into Three Piles
paragraphs: Expunction may be available when the charge was dismissed, you were found not guilty, the grand jury no-billed the case, you were arrested but never charged and the applicable waiting period has passed, or you completed a Class C deferred disposition — which is exactly what many of our traffic and Class C misdemeanor clients end up with. Expunction is generally not available for a case that ended in a conviction or in deferred adjudication for a Class B or higher offense.

Nondisclosure may be available after a completed deferred adjudication for many misdemeanors and some felonies, often after a waiting period, and for certain first-time misdemeanor convictions after the sentence is complete. Family-violence findings, sex offenses and a few other categories are excluded or restricted. Our deferred adjudication record cleanup page walks through the common El Paso scenario: a plea taken years ago, probation completed, and a record that still shows an arrest to anyone who runs it.

sections.heading: The El Paso Employers That Run the Deepest Checks
paragraphs: El Paso's biggest employers run thorough background checks. Fort Bliss and its contractors require security clearances that ask about arrests, charged or not. The federal agencies at the ports of entry and the federal courthouse screen applicants against the full FBI identification record. The hospitals, the Texas Board of Nursing, the school districts and the state licensing boards pull records before issuing a credential — and a dismissed case that was never expunged still shows the arrest. We have seen an old Class C deferral slow a licensing application and a dropped misdemeanor delay a federal start date.

Apartment complexes and credit unions run checks too. The practical rule is that any record you can clear, you should clear before you apply, because explaining it afterward is harder than having it never appear. An expunction removes it from the public databases the commercial background-check companies scrape; a nondisclosure keeps it from private employers, which for many people is the group that matters. Federal forms have their own disclosure rules, and we go over the specific form with you before you submit it.

sections.heading: How the Review Works, Which Page to Read, and What to Send
paragraphs: The first step is a free records review. We pull your El Paso County and DPS history, identify each case and how it ended, and tell you which remedy, if any, appears to apply and when. If you qualify, we draft and file the petition in the district court for an expunction or in the court that heard the case for an order of nondisclosure, give notice to the agencies, and attend the hearing — many are granted without objection. After the order is signed we send certified copies to every agency named and confirm the record has been pulled. Timing depends on the court's docket and the agencies' responses; timing cannot be promised.

If your case ended in a dismissal or a Class C deferral — including a traffic ticket resolved by deferred disposition — read the expunction page. If it ended in deferred adjudication probation or a first conviction, read the nondisclosure page. If you are not sure what happened, or there are several old cases, start with deferred adjudication record cleanup. To start the review, send us any court paperwork you kept — the dismissal, judgment or discharge order — a photo of your driver's license, and the background report if an employer showed you one. Se habla español. This page is general information, not legal advice about your case; the review is free, so reach out before you fill out that application.

faqs.q: What is the difference between an expunction and an order of nondisclosure?
faqs.a: An expunction destroys the record and in general lets you lawfully deny the arrest; it is only for cases that ended without a conviction. A nondisclosure seals the record from the public and private employers while government agencies retain access; it is the tool for many completed deferred adjudications and some convictions.

faqs.q: Can a traffic ticket be expunged in Texas?
faqs.a: Generally yes, if it ended in a dismissal or a completed Class C deferred disposition rather than a paid conviction. That is one more reason not to just pay a ticket — a conviction generally cannot be expunged, but a completed deferral can be.

faqs.q: Will an expunction or nondisclosure clear a federal or Fort Bliss background check?
faqs.a: An expunction removes the record from state and local databases and DPS. Federal clearance questionnaires have their own disclosure rules, so we go over exactly what you may and may not say on each form before you submit it.

The records review is free. After we confirm eligibility we quote a flat fee that covers drafting, filing, the hearing and the agency notices; the court filing fee is set by the court and separate. You will know the total before we start.
